elements.id-string-2: \abstract{In the short time to maturity limit it is proved that for the conditionally lognormal SABR model the zero vanna implied volatility is a lower bound for the volatility swap strike.
elements.id-string-3: The result is valid for all values of the correlation parameter and is a sharper lower bound than the at-the-money implied volatility for correlation less than or equal to zero.}
elements.id-string-5: Liquid instruments to manage volatility risk include variance and volatility swaps.
elements.id-string-6: The former is substantially easier to price than the latter because volatility swaps are more exposed to model risk.
elements.id-string-7: From a risk management and pricing standpoint it is therefore desirable to have robust apprroximations and bounds for volatility swap prices.
elements.id-string-8: One robust approximation is given in the important paper of Carr and Lee \cite{CL1}.
elements.id-string-9: By making use of an immunization technique, and assuming that the skew is generated by a stochastic volatility (SV) model, Carr and Lee were able to give an approximate price for the volatility swap with an error of $\mathrm O(\rho^2)$.
elements.id-string-10: Even though their result is approximate when correlation is nonzero, it remains an important result as the approximation is independent of the specific form of the SV model.
elements.id-string-11: A more recent approximation for the volatility swap is given by Rolloos and Arslan \cite{RA}.
elements.id-string-12: In the aforementioned paper it is shown that the zero vanna implied volatility (ZVIV) approximates the volatility swap price.
elements.id-string-13: The error between the exact volatility swap price and the ZVIV was made precise by Al\`os et al. \cite{ARS} by making use of techniques from Malliavin calculus.
elements.id-string-14: As the volatility swap price is model-dependent, the error between the ZVIV and the exact price will depend on the particular SV model.
elements.id-string-15: In the aforementioned paper by Al\`os et al. numerical simulations indicate that in addition to approximating volatility swaps the ZVIV is also a lower bound for the volatility swap.
elements.id-string-16: In this paper it is proved that for the lognormal SABR model (henceforth SABR model) this is indeed the case for all values of correlation in the short time to maturity limit.
elements.id-string-17: To the best of our knowledge this has not been proved yet in the literature on derivatives pricing.
elements.id-string-18: A proof for general SV models is a subject of future research.
elements.id-string-19: The structure of the note is as follows.
elements.id-string-20: In Section 2 the working assumptions are stated and relevant notation introduced.
elements.id-string-21: Section 3 treats the zero correlation case.
elements.id-string-22: It is proved that both the at-the-money implied volatility (ATMI) and ZVIV are lower bounds for the volatility swap in the short maturity limit in the SABR model.
elements.id-string-23: By making use of the result that the ZVIV is a better approximation than the ATMI it follows that the ZVIV is a sharper lower bound.
elements.id-string-24: The nonzero correlation case is discussed in Section 4, wherein it is proved that in the SABR model the ZVIV is a lower bound for the volatility swap price for any value of correlation.
elements.id-string-25: Furthermore, it is shown that for non-positive correlation it is a sharper lower bound than the ATMI.

elements.id-string-137: It has been shown that in the conditionally lognormal SABR model, the ZVIV is a lower bound for the volatility swap strike for all values of correlation in the short time to maturity limit.
elements.id-string-138: This property, in addition to the results in \cite{ARS}, further cements the ZVIV as a more accurate model-free approximation for the volatility swap strike than the ATMI.
elements.id-string-139: The results in this paper is a first step in analyzing the question for which models the ZVIV is a lower bound for the volatility swap strike.
elements.id-string-140: Further research into the ZVIV as a lower bound for the volatility swap strike will have to includes analyses along the dimensions of the Hurst parameter, correlation parameter and time to maturity.
elements.id-string-141: \abstract{In the short time to maturity limit, it is proved that for the conditionally lognormal SABR model, the zero vanna implied volatility is a lower bound for the volatility swap strike.
elements.id-string-142: In their seminal work Carr and Lee \cite{CL1} prove that for stochastic volatility models, with zero correlation between the spot price and its instantaneous volatility, general volatility derivatives can be priced in a model-free manner.
elements.id-string-143: This is a surprising and important result as prior to Carr and Lee's result it was believed that volatility derivatives other than the log-contract are highly model-dependent.
elements.id-string-144: Indeed, precisely because of its model independence one of the first volatility derivatives to be traded in the market was the variance swap, which is equivalent to the log-contract.
elements.id-string-145: When correlation is non-zero prices of general volatility derivatives do become model-dependent.
elements.id-string-146: Nevertheless, Carr and Lee proved that the model-dependence is of the order $O(\rho^2)$.
elements.id-string-147: Theoretically, their result paves the way for pricing and replicating all European type volatility derivatives with an error of $O(\rho^2)$.
elements.id-string-148: However, as shown by Friz and Gatheral \cite{FG} even in the zero correlation case, pricing volatility options using the Carr and Lee immunisation method leads to highly oscillatory integrals which need regularisation techniques to evaluate.
elements.id-string-149: Furthermore, even for the relatively simple but important volatility swap, the Carr-Lee's pricing method requires a continuum of vanilla options (strikes from $0$ to $\infty$) .
elements.id-string-150: A more recent and straightforward approximation for the volatility swap is given by Rolloos and Arslan \cite{RA}.
elements.id-string-151: In the aforementioned paper, it is shown that the so-called zero vanna implied volatility (ZVIV) approximates the volatility swap price.
elements.id-string-152: In contrast to the Carr-Lee method, the ZVIV approximation does not require a continuum of options, but only one option.
elements.id-string-153: It therefore simplifies the approximate pricing of volatility swaps and is not prone to extrapolation error.
elements.id-string-154: The error between the exact volatility swap price and the ZVIV in the short time to maturity limit was made precise by Al\`os et al. \cite{ARS} for a class of models that include in particular the lognormal SABR, by making use of techniques from the Malliavin calculus.
elements.id-string-155: In their paper Al\`os et al. quantify the error for general stochastic volatility models driven by fractional noise.
elements.id-string-156: Recent studies \cite{CR,GJR} have argued for the relevance of fractional noise in explaining the shape of the implied volatility skew.
elements.id-string-157: In Al\`os et al. numerical simulations also indicate that, in addition to approximating volatility swaps, the ZVIV is a lower bound for the volatility swap.
elements.id-string-158: In this paper it is proved that for the lognormal SABR model (henceforth SABR model), this is indeed the case for all values of correlation in the short time to maturity limit.

elements.id-string-220: In the previous sections it has been proved that in the short time to maturity limit the ZVIV bounds the volatility swap price from below.
elements.id-string-221: For longer time to maturities the numerical experiments in this section suggests that the ZVIV remains a lower bound.
elements.id-string-222: A proof of this conjecture, however, is currently not known.
elements.id-string-223: For the numerical experiments the volatility swap strike, the ZVIV and the ATMI are calculated for various values of volatility of volatility and time to maturity:
elements.id-string-225: The values of correlation are set in 0.1 increments from -1 to 1, and the initial value of the volatility is $\sigma_0 = 0.3$.
elements.id-string-226: In order to calculate the volatility swap strike, the ZVIV and ATMI, $10^7$ simulations are carried out for each value of $\rho, \alpha$ and $T$.
elements.id-string-227: The results are depicted in Figures 1 to 4.
elements.id-string-228: As can be deduced from the figures, and in line with the results of the previous sections and in \cite{ARS}, the ZVIV is indeed a more accurate approximation for the volatility swap price than the ATMI.
elements.id-string-229: Furthermore the impact of correlation on ZVIV is almost of second order.
elements.id-string-230: The term 'almost' is used since the ZVIV approximation is obtained by Taylor approximations in \cite{RA}.
elements.id-string-231: Thus there are still residual terms of $O(\rho)$ that remain in the ZVIV.
elements.id-string-232: The impact of these terms is apparent for longer time to maturities, significant nonzero values for correlation, and high volatility of volatility as in Figure 4.
elements.id-string-233: We can also clearly see in Figure 4 that for $\rho = 0$ the ZVIV is not exactly equal to the volatility swap strike.
elements.id-string-234: This is another manifestation of the fact that there are small residual terms of  $O(\rho)$ present in the ZVIV.
